```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

Lag sequential analysis starts from one table: the counts $O_{ij}$ of how
often state $i$ was followed by state $j$ at a given lag. Several classical
tests can be computed from that table, and they answer different questions.
The classical test asks whether a directed transition $i \to j$ occurs more or
less often than the base rates of $i$ and $j$ predict (Bakeman & Quera, 2011).
The two-cell test asks the same question through the odds ratio of a
$2 \times 2$ collapse (Bakeman & Gottman, 1997). The bidirectional test drops
direction and asks whether the pair $\{i, j\}$ co-occurs more than expected.
The two dominance tests ask whether, within the pair, $i \to j$ outnumbers
$j \to i$ (Sackett, 1979; Wampold, 1984).

In `lagdynamics` each of these tests is an *engine*: a function that takes the
transition table and returns per-cell statistics. Every engine is reached
through `lsa(data, engine = )` or through a wrapper with the engine fixed
(`lsa_classical()`, `lsa_two_cell()`, `lsa_bidirectional()`,
`lsa_parallel_dominance()`, `lsa_nonparallel_dominance()`), and every fit is
read with the same verbs: `transitions()`, `tests()`, `plot()`. This guide
gives, for each engine, the statistic, the null hypothesis, the columns it
adds to `transitions()`, and the question it answers. It then fits all five on
the same data, shows where they agree and where they part ways, and ends with
how to register an engine of your own. The model and its reading verbs are
introduced in [the LSA vignette](lsa.html); structural zeros, which only the
classical engine supports, are covered in
[the lags and structural zeros guide](lags-structural-zeros.html).

```{r package}
library(lagdynamics)
```

## Data

Two bundled datasets are used.

- **`engagement`**: weekly engagement states of 138 students over 15 weeks,
  one row per student (wide format). States: `Active`, `Average`,
  `Disengaged`. Two rows are entirely missing, so fits use 136 sequences.
  With three states each table has nine cells, small enough to print in full.
- **`group_regulation`**: coded regulation actions in 2,000 collaborative
  learning sessions, one row per group session and one column per ordered
  time point (`T1` to `T26`, shorter sessions padded with `NA`). Nine
  states: `adapt`, `cohesion`, `consensus`, `coregulate`, `discuss`,
  `emotion`, `monitor`, `plan`, `synthesis`. Used to compare the engines on a
  larger table.

The registry lists the engines available in the session.

```{r registry}
list_lsa_engines()
```

The five built-in engines are registered when the package loads. Any engine
added with `register_lsa_engine()` appears in the same table.

## Classical: adjusted residuals under independence

The classical engine tests each directed cell against sequential
independence. With row totals $R_i$, column totals $C_j$ and $N$ transitions,
the expected count and the adjusted residual (Haberman, 1973) are

$$E_{ij} = \frac{R_i C_j}{N}, \qquad
z_{ij} = \frac{O_{ij} - E_{ij}}{\sqrt{E_{ij}\,(1 - R_i/N)\,(1 - C_j/N)}}.$$

The null for each cell is that the next state does not depend on the current
one; $z_{ij}$ is referred to the standard normal. Alongside the residual, the
engine reports Yule's $Q = (ad - bc)/(ad + bc)$ from the $2 \times 2$
collapse of the cell ($a = O_{ij}$, $b = R_i - O_{ij}$, $c = C_j - O_{ij}$,
$d = N - R_i - C_j + O_{ij}$), Wampold's unidirectional kappa with its own $z$
and $p$ (computed from event totals rather than transition totals), and the
tablewise likelihood-ratio $G^2 = 2\sum O \log(O/E)$ and Pearson $X^2$ tests
with $(K-1)^2$ degrees of freedom. It is the only engine that supports
structural zeros.

```{r classical}
fit_classical <- lsa_classical(engagement)
fit_classical
transitions(fit_classical)
tests(fit_classical)
```

Seven of the nine transitions depart from independence. The three
self-transitions are the over-represented cells (Active to Active,
$z = 21.7$, 459 observed against 247 expected), and every move between
`Active` and the other two states is under-represented. The two transitions
out of `Disengaged` into `Average` and out of `Average` into `Disengaged` are
the only ones consistent with independence ($z = -1.74$ and $z = 0.18$). The
tablewise test rejects independence for the table as a whole
($G^2 = 618$, df = 4). The answer to the classical question is that weekly
engagement is sticky: students tend to stay where they are, and direct moves
between `Active` and `Disengaged` are rare (23 and 39 transitions against
expectations of 121 and 122).

## Two-cell: the log odds ratio

The two-cell engine collapses each cell into the same $2 \times 2$ table
($a, b, c, d$ above) and tests the odds ratio $OR = ad/(bc)$ with a Wald test
on its logarithm:

$$z_{ij} = \frac{\log OR_{ij}}{\sqrt{1/a + 1/b + 1/c + 1/d}}.$$

When any of the four counts is zero, 0.5 is added to all four (the
Haldane-Anscombe correction; the amount is the engine parameter
`continuity`). The null is $OR = 1$: being in state $i$ does not change the
odds that the next state is $j$. The residual column `adj_res` holds this Wald
$z$, and the engine appends `odds_ratio`, `log_or` and `log_or_se`. Kappa is
not computed and there is no tablewise test.

```{r two-cell}
transitions(lsa_two_cell(engagement))
```

The two-cell test flags the same seven transitions as the classical test, with
the same signs, and its Yule's Q column is identical because both engines
compute $Q$ from the same collapse. The $z$ values are close but not equal
(Active to Active: 20.3 against 21.7) because the Wald statistic uses the
standard error of the log odds ratio rather than the expected-count variance.
The engine earns its place through its effect size: an odds ratio of 10.6 for
Active to Active says that an active week multiplies the odds of another
active week by more than ten, and an odds ratio of 0.095 for Active to
Disengaged says that an active week cuts the odds of a disengaged one by about
a factor of ten.

## Bidirectional: the unordered pair

The bidirectional engine asks whether two states follow each other in either
order more often than expected. It symmetrises the table, $W = O + O^\top$,
and computes adjusted residuals on $W$ with symmetric margins
$R^W_i = \sum_j W_{ij}$:

$$E^W_{ij} = \frac{R^W_i R^W_j}{N_W}, \qquad
z_{ij} = \frac{W_{ij} - E^W_{ij}}{\sqrt{E^W_{ij}\,(1 - R^W_i/N_W)\,(1 - R^W_j/N_W)}}.$$

The statistic is symmetric, so the rows $i \to j$ and $j \to i$ carry the
same `adj_res` and `p`; the fit is marked undirected. A diagonal cell of $W$
is twice the self-transition count. The engine appends `symmetric_obs`
($W_{ij}$) and `symmetric_exp` ($E^W_{ij}$); `expected` also holds
$E^W_{ij}$. The `count`, `prob`, `lift` and `sign` columns are computed from
the directed counts, so the bidirectional result is read from `adj_res`,
`symmetric_obs` and `symmetric_exp`, not from `lift` or `sign`.

```{r bidirectional}
transitions(lsa_bidirectional(engagement))
```

The pair `Active`/`Disengaged` occurs 62 times in either order against 243
expected ($z = -16.3$), and the pair `Active`/`Average` 329 times against 571
($z = -17.1$). The pair `Average`/`Disengaged` is not distinguishable from
independence ($z = -1.11$). The bidirectional reading agrees with the
classical one but compresses it: the classical engine needed two cells to
say that `Active` and `Disengaged` avoid each other, the bidirectional engine
says it once.

## Dominance: which direction wins within a pair

The dominance engines take each pair of states and ask whether one direction
outnumbers the other. Both use the difference $D_{ij} = O_{ij} - O_{ji}$ and
differ in its standard error. The parallel-dominance engine scales by the
counts expected under independence,

$$z_{ij} = \frac{O_{ij} - O_{ji}}{\sqrt{E_{ij} + E_{ji}}},$$

and the non-parallel-dominance engine scales by the observed pair total,

$$z_{ij} = \frac{O_{ij} - O_{ji}}{\sqrt{O_{ij} + O_{ji}}},$$

which is the normal approximation to the exact test of
$O_{ij} \sim \text{Binomial}(O_{ij} + O_{ji}, 1/2)$; that exact p-value is
also returned. The null is symmetry within the pair: $i \to j$ and $j \to i$
are equally likely. The statistic is antisymmetric ($z_{ij} = -z_{ji}$) and a
self-transition has no direction, so the diagonal is $z = 0$, $p = 1$. Both
engines put the dominance $z$ in `adj_res` and append `dominance` ($D_{ij}$);
the parallel engine adds `dominance_se`, the non-parallel engine adds
`pair_totals` and `binomial_p`. The `expected`, `lift` and `sign` columns
still describe the independence model, not the dominance test.

```{r parallel}
transitions(lsa_parallel_dominance(engagement))
```

No pair has a dominant direction under the parallel test. The largest count
difference is between `Active` and `Average` ($D = 23$, $z = 0.96$): students
move from `Active` down to `Average` 176 times and back up 153 times, a
difference well within chance.

```{r nonparallel}
transitions(lsa_nonparallel_dominance(engagement))
```

The non-parallel test flags one pair: `Disengaged` to `Active` outnumbers
`Active` to `Disengaged`, 39 against 23 ($D = 16$, $z = 2.03$, $p = 0.042$).
The two dominance tests differ here because the pair is rare. Under
independence the pair would occur 243 times, so the parallel standard error is
$\sqrt{243} = 15.6$; it actually occurs 62 times, so the non-parallel standard
error is $\sqrt{62} = 7.87$. The exact binomial p-value for the same pair is
0.056, above 0.05, while the `significant` column follows the normal $p$.
With a pair total of 62 the exact test is the one to report, and it does not
support a dominant direction: direct jumps between `Active` and `Disengaged`
run upward somewhat more often than downward, but not reliably so.

## Where the engines agree and disagree

On the larger `group_regulation` table the engines can be compared on the
transitions they rank first. The classical and two-cell engines are printed
first.

```{r gr-classical}
fit_gr <- lsa_classical(group_regulation)
transitions(fit_gr, significant = TRUE, sort = "strength") |> head(6)
transitions(lsa_two_cell(group_regulation), significant = TRUE,
            sort = "strength") |> head(6)
```

Both engines rank `emotion -> cohesion` first (classical $z = 58.2$, two-cell
$z = 48.0$) and agree on the sign of every listed cell, but their orderings
differ below the top: the classical engine puts `synthesis -> adapt` third and
`discuss -> plan` fourth, the two-cell engine puts `consensus -> coregulate`
third and `consensus -> consensus` fourth. The Wald $z$ falls furthest below
the adjusted residual for the most lopsided cells: `discuss -> synthesis`
(odds ratio 26.5) drops from 48.0 to 33.3 and `synthesis -> adapt` from 38.8
to 28.2, while `consensus -> coregulate` (odds ratio 4.66) moves only from
35.3 to 32.9. The classical $z$ is the statistic to rank by; the odds ratio is
the effect size to report next to it.

The bidirectional engine ranks pairs, so its top rows come in mirrored
pairs.

```{r gr-bidirectional}
transitions(lsa_bidirectional(group_regulation), significant = TRUE,
            sort = "strength") |> head(6)
```

The strongest bidirectional result is a self-transition: `consensus` follows
itself far less often than independence predicts ($z = -50.2$). The pair
`emotion`/`cohesion` follows ($z = 42.2$), with 923 transitions one way and
196 the other. The pair `plan`/`discuss` is avoided in both directions
($z = -41.3$). The bidirectional view hides the fact that `emotion -> cohesion`
is the dominant direction of the pair, which is the question the dominance
engines answer.

```{r gr-dominance}
transitions(lsa_parallel_dominance(group_regulation), direction = "over",
            sort = "strength") |> head(5)
transitions(lsa_nonparallel_dominance(group_regulation), direction = "over",
            sort = "strength") |> head(5)
```

With `direction = "over"`, each pair appears once, in its dominant direction.
The parallel test ranks `emotion -> cohesion` first ($D = 727$, $z = 37.5$)
and the non-parallel test ranks `cohesion -> consensus` first ($D = 750$,
$z = 24.5$). Both sets point the same way: the turn-taking of these groups
runs from emotion to cohesion, from cohesion to consensus, from consensus to
coregulation, and from discussion to synthesis, much more than the reverse.
The two tests disagree on order because the parallel standard error is large
for pairs that independence expects often and small for pairs it expects
rarely, which promotes `synthesis -> adapt` ($D = 153$, $z = 29.3$, all 153
transitions of the pair in one direction) to third place.

A residual heatmap of the classical fit and of the parallel-dominance fit
shows the difference in what the two engines test. The classical map has its
strongest cells wherever a transition is common or rare relative to the base
rates; the dominance map is antisymmetric, with each over-represented cell
mirrored by an under-represented one across the diagonal.

```{r heatmap-classical, fig.height = 5}
plot(fit_gr)
```

```{r heatmap-dominance, fig.height = 5}
plot(lsa_parallel_dominance(group_regulation))
```

The dominance map mirrors itself: `consensus -> coregulate` is $+29.03$ and
`coregulate -> consensus` is $-29.03$, and the diagonal is 0. The cells that
dominate are not the cells that are most over-represented: `consensus -> plan`
is the fifth largest positive cell of the classical map (32.58) but only 12.93 in
the dominance map, because `plan -> consensus` is common too. The three grey
cells in both maps are transitions with no observed count, which the heatmap
leaves blank.

## Writing your own engine

The registry is open. An engine is a function that accepts `transitions`
(the `lsa_transitions` object of counts) and `...`, and returns a named list
with at least the $K \times K$ matrices `obs`, `exp`, `prob`, `adj_res` and
`p`. Any further $K \times K$ matrix it returns becomes an extra column of
`transitions()`. The example below defines Pearson residuals,
$(O - E)/\sqrt{E}$, which omit the margin correction of the adjusted residual.

```{r custom-engine}
pearson_engine <- function(transitions, ...) {
  obs <- transitions$obs
  expected <- outer(rowSums(obs), colSums(obs)) / sum(obs)
  residual <- (obs - expected) / sqrt(expected)
  list(obs = obs, exp = expected, prob = obs / rowSums(obs),
       adj_res = residual, p = 2 * stats::pnorm(-abs(residual)))
}
register_lsa_engine("pearson", pearson_engine,
                    description = "Pearson residuals under independence")
list_lsa_engines()
transitions(lsa(engagement, engine = "pearson"), significant = TRUE)
```

The Pearson engine flags the same seven transitions as the classical engine,
with smaller values (Active to Active: 13.5 against 21.7), because the
adjusted residual divides by the smaller standard deviation that accounts for
the fixed margins. The Pearson residual is not standard normal under the null
and understates departures; it is shown here as a template, not as an
alternative to the classical engine. Columns the engine did not return, such
as Yule's Q and kappa, are `NA`. An engine stays registered for the session;
remove it with `unregister_lsa_engine()`.

```{r unregister}
unregister_lsa_engine("pearson")
```

## Which engine to use

| Question | Engine | Statistic in `adj_res` | Extra columns |
|---|---|---|---|
| Does $i \to j$ occur more or less than base rates predict? | `classical` | adjusted residual | kappa, `kappa_z`, `kappa_p`; tablewise tests |
| How large is that association, as an odds ratio? | `two_cell` | Wald $z$ of $\log OR$ | `odds_ratio`, `log_or`, `log_or_se` |
| Do $i$ and $j$ follow each other, in either order, more than expected? | `bidirectional` | adjusted residual of $O + O^\top$ | `symmetric_obs`, `symmetric_exp` |
| Within a pair, does one direction outnumber the other? (common pairs) | `parallel_dominance` | $D/\sqrt{E_{ij}+E_{ji}}$ | `dominance`, `dominance_se` |
| The same, for rare pairs | `nonparallel_dominance` | $D/\sqrt{O_{ij}+O_{ji}}$ | `dominance`, `pair_totals`, `binomial_p` |

The classical engine is the default and the one every inference verb
(bootstrap, permutation, group comparison) is built around; start there. Add
the two-cell engine when an effect size on the odds scale is needed for
reporting. Use the bidirectional engine when the coding does not fix
direction (two partners whose turns alternate) or when the question is about
pairing rather than sequence. Use a dominance engine when the question is
about direction within a pair, as in who leads and who follows; prefer the
non-parallel engine and its exact `binomial_p` when pair totals are small.
Only the classical engine supports structural zeros (`loops = FALSE` or a
`structural_zeros` matrix); the others stop with an error of class
`lagdynamics_unsupported_option`.

## References

Bakeman, R., & Gottman, J. M. (1997). *Observing interaction: An introduction
to sequential analysis* (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press.

Bakeman, R., & Quera, V. (2011). *Sequential analysis and observational
methods for the behavioral sciences*. Cambridge University Press.

Haberman, S. J. (1973). The analysis of residuals in cross-classified tables.
*Biometrics, 29*, 205-220.

Sackett, G. P. (1979). The lag sequential analysis of contingency and
cyclicity in behavioral interaction research. In J. D. Osofsky (Ed.),
*Handbook of infant development* (pp. 623-649). Wiley.

Wampold, B. E. (1984). Tests of dominance in sequential categorical data.
*Psychological Bulletin, 96*(2), 424-429.
